doc.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003

title: No greatest in jazz; method books, smooth jazz and Herbie Hancock
summary: He praises Herbie Hancock's thematic albums, rejects the idea of a greatest player, and says books like Baker's only offer tools to find identity.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

And they were saying that every week they get flooded with CDs from people they never even heard of. And they put on some of them and they are terrible. But what can you do? People have access to make them. And I think that the albums I’ve made I put a lot of thought into. And this is one of the things I admired about Herbie Hancock when he started doing his thing. Herbie always had a theme and he was always centering his thing, of all the records he would put out so that they made statements. And I think that Herbie has always been a young genius about that. And he’s another one, like a young guy who came along that had a lot of stuff going on. But he also gave deference to the Red Garlands, the Tommy Flanagans, the Hank Jones, the Wynton Kellys, Bill Evans, etc. Because we have to understand. And the people that want to say this guy was the greatest — there is no such thing as the greatest in jazz. There is no such animal. Coleman Hawkins is Coleman Hawkins, John Coltrane is John Coltrane. Stan Getz is Stan Getz. We have to understand that these people reached the ultimate goal that I feel that’s what’s happening in jazz. Finding one’s signature and personal identity. And if you’re not in a quest for that you are missing the boat. And if the teachers and the professors that are counseling these young people, if they’re not teaching along those lines, if they’re not using those method books that we’re talking about that have become a part of the publishing side of jazz education and the music industry, and these people that publish these books, they’ve got to step off their high horse too. They haven’t written the Bible of jazz improvisation. That’s just one person’s interpretation in an attempt to codify. The only books that I would say that kind of rank up there, the tablets that Moses brought down from Mt. Sinai, the David Bakers and the Jerry Cokers and the John Mehegan books, and a few others, I mean I mention that because these are the guys that were at the very beginning of it. And if you haven’t attempt to follow in the line of where they were coming from of trying to give people the tools to find their own identity, then you’re missing the boat. Because just having someone come and being a carbon copy just ‘cause they can play a few licks and sound jazzy is not playing jazz. And the smooth jazz players, they’ve got to recognize that too. They’ve got to come back. I’m tired of hearing these guys sound like they’re playing with a two by four on the alto and they’ve all got the same harsh, guttural sound. It’s very saccharin. They need to listen to Johnny Hodges and hear the difference between his sound versus a Marshall Royal, versus a Charlie Parker, versus a Jackie McLean or any other alto saxophonist. Paul Desmond even. Paul had his own sound and I applaud Paul. Because Paul wasn’t trying to sound like Charlie Parker. Charlie Parker liked Lee Konitz. These guys had their own thing.
